title: One Rust Unicode Bug, Three Coding Models: A Reproducible Comparison

content_html:
Coding-model leaderboards reveal little about how a model handles a real bug. A Rust function can work on ASCII and still panic on valid Unicode because it slices UTF-8 at the wrong byte boundary. The fix must respect character boundaries and preserve the &str return type. This article uses one reproducible bug, one prompt, and the same regression tests to compare three models on the quality of their patches, not the confidence of their explanations.

A one-line Rust slice can panic on valid UTF-8. That makes it a useful coding-model challenge. The fix must preserve the function signature, handle character boundaries, and pass regression tests. This comparison uses the same bug for three models and judges their patches using compiler output rather than leaderboard scores.

The bug

The function below is supposed to return the first n characters of a string. It works on plain ASCII and panics when n cuts through a multibyte UTF-8 character.

pub fn prefix(input: &str, n: usize) -> &str {
    if n >= input.len() {
        return input;
    }
    &input[..n]
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::prefix;

    #[test]
    fn ascii() {
        assert_eq!(prefix("rustacean", 4), "rust");
    }

    #[test]
    fn unicode() {
        assert_eq!(prefix("café", 4), "café");
    }

    #[test]
    fn beyond_length() {
        assert_eq!(prefix("é", 10), "é");
    }
}

The original implementation counts bytes, not characters. In UTF-8, the final é in café occupies two bytes. Slicing at byte index four cuts through that character and panics. Save the code as src/lib.rs in a new Cargo library project. Run cargo test to reproduce the failing Unicode case.

Three models, one task

The three candidates are DeepSeek V4 Pro, Claude Fable 5.1, and Grok Build 0.1. These are the target model pages for the comparison. Model availability, exact API identifiers, and supported parameters must be checked against the live catalog before execution.

Model API identifier Temperature Input Version
DeepSeek V4 Pro Confirm from catalog 0 Same Rust file and prompt Record API version
Claude Fable 5.1 Confirm from catalog 0 Same Rust file and prompt Record API version
Grok Build 0.1 Confirm from catalog 0 Same Rust file and prompt Record API version

Use the same request body, system instructions, maximum output allowance, and test environment for every model. Record the exact model ID returned by the API. A zero temperature reduces randomness but does not guarantee identical answers on repeated calls.

The prompt

Use the following prompt unchanged for every model.

Fix the Rust function below. It must return the first n Unicode scalar values without panicking. Keep the return type &str. Explain the bug briefly, return a complete src/lib.rs, and add a regression test for an emoji and a combining character. Do not add external dependencies.

Append the entire original src/lib.rs after that instruction. Do not tell one model about another model's failure. Do not silently repair a response before testing.

What to inspect in each model's patch

DeepSeek V4 Pro

Capture the raw response, its reported input and output tokens, the elapsed request time, and the first cargo test output. A correct patch should iterate over char boundaries rather than slice at an arbitrary byte index. If the returned code does not compile, retain the error and count the next prompt as another attempt. Add a screenshot of the response and terminal output from the actual run.

Claude Fable 5.1

Use the identical source and prompt. Record whether the model preserves the borrowed &str return type and whether it handles a request longer than the character count. Check the combining-character case carefully. Unicode scalar values are not the same as grapheme clusters. A request for one scalar value from an e followed by a combining accent may return only the e. That is correct under this task's definition.

Grok Build 0.1

Repeat the procedure without editing the prompt. Review whether the model changes the API, introduces a dependency, or returns a String instead of &str. These changes matter even when the visible output looks correct. Keep the first attempt and any follow-up attempts as separate records.

What a correct fix looks like

One valid approach uses char_indices to find the byte boundary after the requested number of scalar values.

pub fn prefix(input: &str, n: usize) -> &str {
    let end = input
        .char_indices()
        .nth(n)
        .map(|(index, _)| index)
        .unwrap_or(input.len());
    &input[..end]
}

This reference implementation is a correctness oracle for the exercise, not an attributed output from any model. The test suite should include ASCII, multibyte characters, empty strings, n equal to zero, n greater than the character count, emoji, and decomposed accents. The reference code should be kept out of model prompts.

The scorecard becomes useful once each row is populated from the first response, Cargo output, and API logs. Until then, it is a repeatable evaluation worksheet rather than a model ranking.

What to pick for each coding task

For short patches, first-pass compilation and correct edge cases matter more than a polished explanation. For larger refactors, examine how often a model changes unrelated code. For code review, test whether it identifies the byte-versus-character distinction without prompting. For terminal automation, compare how predictably each model follows the required output format.

The best LLM for coding is task dependent. One Rust bug cannot establish which model performs best across a whole repository, language, or toolchain. It can reveal whether a model handles a concrete failure mode under controlled conditions.

How to repeat the comparison

Create a Cargo library with cargo new unicode-prefix --lib. Replace src/lib.rs with the buggy example and run cargo test. Send the same prompt and file to each confirmed model identifier. Save the raw JSON response, request timestamp, token usage fields, and model version. Extract the proposed code into a clean working tree for each attempt. Run cargo fmt --check, cargo test, and cargo clippy. Record failures without modifying the first answer.

Keep the repository organized as follows:

baseline/src/lib.rs
oracle/src/lib.rs
prompts/task.txt
runs/<model>/response.json
runs/<model>/cargo-test.txt

Publish a repository link only after the files are uploaded. The reproducible artifact is the code and logs, not a ranking graphic.

A shareable comparison includes the repository, unedited first responses, and Cargo logs. Readers can inspect both the proposed fixes and the failures.

Create a Cargo library with cargo new unicode-prefix --lib. Replace src/lib.rs with the buggy example and run cargo test. Send the same prompt and file to each confirmed model identifier. Save the raw JSON response, request timestamp, token usage fields, and model version. Extract the proposed code into a clean working tree for each attempt. Run cargo fmt --check, cargo test, and cargo clippy. Record failures without modifying the first answer.

Keep the repository organized as follows:

baseline/src/lib.rs
oracle/src/lib.rs
prompts/task.txt
runs/<model>/response.json
runs/<model>/cargo-test.txt

Publish a repository link only after the files are uploaded. The reproducible artifact is the code and logs, not a ranking graphic.

A shareable comparison includes the repository, unedited first responses, and Cargo logs. Readers can inspect both the proposed fixes and the failures.
